newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Wildlife flourishes in Berlin Death Strip.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Wildlife flourishes in Berlin Death Strip.

text.p: The "Death Strip" next to the Berlin Wall was for years one of the world's most treacherous barriers, but its deathly silence created an improbably fertile habitat for plants and animals.

Although the cement Wall breached on November 9, 1989 has gone, the former "no-man's land" along its path is still intact. And hundreds of species of exotic plant life, including some found usually only near the Mediterranean and Baltic Seas, have found a home in the 100-metre (330-feet) wide corridor.

Disturbed only by sporadic gun shots fired by East German border guards at escaping refugees, the 155 km (96-mile) long green band around West Berlin became a Cold War paradise for insects, plants, birds and animals.
They profited from the relative warmth of the inner city climate in a silent zone where they did not have to contend with the commotion of humans.

"The area was generally warmer because of its proximity to the city, it was dry and almost never disturbed by humans," said Susanne Sarlinger, a biologist for the environmental protection association (BUND).

"It is ironic and even absurd when you think about it -- we have all this life and fresh air in the middle of the city now because of the death strip. For all the wrong reasons, we have this wonderful green ring."
It may not have made the front pages in Berlin when non-indigenous insects such as the tiger beetle, or birds like the wheatear or kingfisher were spotted for the first time.
But reports of foxes and wild boars roaming along the strip near the city centre have made headlines. It is now one of the most closely studied nature habitats in the world.
"There is a huge overpopulation of rabbits in the strip," said Detlev Dahlmann, who is helping build a 1.5 km (one mile) long "Mauerpark" (Wall Park) that preserves part of the belt.
An earlier proposal by environmentalists to preserve the entire 96-mile long strip as a natural biotope, complete with earthen bridges so insects could roam at will, was discarded by city planners.
The barbed wire, attack dogs and landmines are long gone and the area has since become an inner city utopia for joggers, cyclists, walkers, joggers and roller-bladers.
Some segments of the green belt that surrounded West Berlin have been turned into roads, car parks or office buildings.
And even if it is not as quiet as during the Cold War, there is still a dizzying array of flora and fauna that is enthralling botanists and biologists.
A Czech ecologist found 1,432 plant species in Berlin, five times more than any other European city, many near the Wall.
"There was nothing like this death strip biotope anywhere else in the world," said Joerg Goetting-Forsinski, editor of the Berlin environmental magazine Gruenstift.
Werner Schulz, who studied the no-man's land for the "Green League" environmental group, said there are countless forms of plant and animal life not indigenous to Berlin.
"The conditions were ideal for many species," he said. "It was dry and its sandy terrain was a steppe-like grassy plain."
The strip was open and dry because East German border guards cleared trees so they could spot and shoot at would-be refugees. Hundreds were killed trying to escape over the Wall.
The East Germans also used pesticides but, in a bizarre twist, these encouraged plant life normally found only near the Baltic Sea, more than 200 km (120 miles) to the north.
Some plants which need salty soil flourished in the strip because of the pesticides.
"The poisons are long gone from the soil, but there was still enough salt in the ground for plants usually seen only in the Mediterranean region," Schulz said.
But there is another factor behind the diverse vegetation.
Many parts of the Berlin Wall were built next to some of the main rail lines that pass through Berlin. Seeds from all over Europe and Asia "hitchhiked" on freight trains and landed in the city.
After the Wall was built in 1961, the rail lines were idle and the exotic plants flourished.
The Wall was largely successful in keeping Easterners away from West Berlin, but it also had the unintended effect of keeping rodents such as the lesser white-toothed shrew out of West Berlin.
The lesser white-toothed shrew has been wandering northwards from southern Europe for centuries. It reached East Germany and East Berlin in the 1970s, but couldn't find a way past the Berlin Wall.
But within months of the Wall's fall, it accomplished what the Warsaw Pact only dreamed of -- it took Berlin.
